steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm single, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $79,400 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing graphic design for 4 clients, got $890 interest from Discover Bank savings and $480 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $720 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — useful detail. Below is a clear, practical summary of what’s deductible, whether to itemize, how to handle the home office, the forms you’ll use, and an estimate of the most important numbers. I’ll note assumptions I made and a few quick questions at the end.

Summary / conclusion (short)
- Likely take the standard deduction (2023 single = $13,850). With the info given, itemized deductions (charity $720 plus typical state tax withholding) probably won’t exceed the standard amount.
- Your graphic-design income is self‑employment income and is reported on Schedule C; business expenses (supplies, home‑office portion of rent) reduce that income.
- Use the actual-method home-office deduction (Form 8829) — it gives a larger deduction here than the simplified method.
- Student loan interest is an above‑the‑line deduction but is phased out by MAGI; with the approximate AGI you’ll only be able to claim a partial amount (not the full $4,800).
- You’ll also owe self‑employment tax on the net business profit (reported on Schedule SE); half of that SE tax is an above‑the‑line deduction.

Key deductible items & where they go
- Self-employment business expenses (Schedule C):
  - Work supplies ($780) — deductible on Schedule C.
  - Home-office deduction — either:
    - Actual method: allocate rent to office (use Form 8829 and transfer result to Schedule C), or
    - Simplified method: $5 × square footage (up to 300 sq ft).
- Half of self-employment tax — above‑the‑line deduction (Schedule 1 to Form 1040).
- Student loan interest — above‑the‑line deduction on Schedule 1 to Form 1040, up to $2,500 but phased out by MAGI. (You likely exceed the threshold enough to be limited — see estimate below.)
- Charitable gift ($720) — only deductible if you itemize (on Schedule A). No above‑the‑line deduction for cash gifts in 2023.

Reporting requirements for the other items
- W-2 wages — reported on Form 1040.
- Self-employment income — Schedule C. If you received any 1099-NEC/1099-MISC, include them; even if you didn’t receive a 1099 you still report all income.
- Self-employment tax — Schedule SE (you pay both income tax and SE tax).
- Interest ($890) and dividends ($480) — reported on Form 1040. (No Schedule B unless interest + dividends > $1,500 or other triggers.)
- Oregon state tax — file Oregon return (OR-40) and include your combined income; state rent is not deductible on federal return, but state income is calculated from federal AGI with state adjustments.

Home office calculation (based on numbers you gave)
- Office area: 165 sq ft; total home: 690 sq ft → business-use percentage = 165 / 690 ≈ 23.9%.
- Annual rent = $2,050 × 12 = $24,600. Home-office share (actual method) = 24,600 × 23.913% ≈ $5,884.
- Simplified method would be 165 × $5 = $825 (actual method gives a much larger deduction).
- Business income and limitation: your gross self-employment receipts $8,900 minus other non-home-office business expenses ($780) = $8,120 available to absorb home-office deduction. The $5,884 home-office deduction is less than that, so it’s allowed (no carryover needed).

Estimated tax-impact (rough calculations / assumptions)
Assumptions: all numbers are for 2023; student-loan interest you listed was paid in 2023; no other major deductions or income not listed.

1) Compute net self-employment profit (using actual home-office):
- Gross self-employment receipts: $8,900
- Less supplies: − $780
- Less home-office portion of rent: − $5,884
- Net profit ≈ $2,236

2) Self-employment tax:
- SE tax ≈ 15.3% × 92.35% × net profit ≈ ~ $316
- Half SE (above-the-line deduction) ≈ $158

3) AGI before student loan deduction:
- W-2 wages: $79,400
- + Net SE income: + $2,236
- + Interest $890 + Dividends $480
- = subtotal ≈ $83,006
- − half SE tax (−$158) → AGI ≈ $82,848

4) Student loan interest deduction (phaseout):
- Phaseout range for single (2023) is MAGI $75,000–$90,000.
- With AGI ≈ $82,848 you are partially phased out: allowed amount ≈ $2,500 × (1 − (82,848 − 75,000) / 15,000) ≈ $1,190 (approx).
- So expected student loan deduction ≈ $1,190 (not the full $4,800).

5) Taxable income (approx):
- AGI after student-loan deduction ≈ $81,658
- − Standard deduction $13,850 → taxable income ≈ $67,808
- Federal income tax (rough bracket calc) ≈ $10,200
- Plus self-employment tax ≈ $316 (note you already got half as deduction)
- These are rough numbers — your W-2 withholding will reduce any balance due / refund.

Forms and worksheets you’ll use
- Form 1040 (main return)
- Schedule 1 (adjustments to income — student loan interest, half SE tax entry flows here)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report self-employment income and business expenses
- Schedule SE (Self-Employment Tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) if using the actual-method home-office deduction. (If you use the simplified method, you don’t file Form 8829; instead you enter the simplified deduction on Schedule C.)
- Schedule A (only if you itemize — e.g., to claim the $720 charitable gift)

Practical recommendations
- Use the actual-method home-office deduction (Form 8829) since it’s substantially larger here.
- Report all self-employment income even if you didn’t get a 1099.
- Take the standard deduction unless you have other itemizable amounts (large state/local taxes, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, etc.) that would push itemizing above $13,850.
- Keep receipts for the charitable gift, student-loan interest statement (Form 1098-E, if you have it), and all business expenses.
- Because your self-employment income is modest, your SE tax is small, but check whether you need to make estimated tax payments next year (or increase withholding) so you don’t get underpayment penalties.
- Consider a tax-prep appointment or software walkthrough to enter actual numbers and get an exact refund/amount due; I can help prepare a more precise worksheet if you want.

A few clarifying questions
1. Were the $4,800 of student-loan interest payments actually paid in 2023 (or are those totals from earlier years)? The deduction applies to interest you paid in the tax year.
2. Does your home office meet the "exclusive and regular use" test (i.e., used only for business and regularly)?
3. Did you receive any 1099-NEC forms from those 4 clients? Any other business expenses besides the $780 in supplies?
4. How much state income tax was withheld on your W-2 (or paid in estimated taxes)? That affects whether itemizing could be better.

Would you like me to:
- Run a precise calculator with the numbers above and any corrections (I can re-run totals if you confirm answers to the questions), or
- Draft a short summary you can send to your accountant with these figures and questions, or
- Create a checklist of receipts/documents to collect before filing?

Which of those would you like next?
